http://www.jpost.com/archaeology/article.text: Archaeologists have uncovered the full floor of Lithuania's historic Great Synagogue, revealing treasures nearly erased by Nazi and Soviet occupations, and exposing rifts between Lithuanian Jews over how to preserve and interpret what survived.Locals walking through the center of Vilnius now pass a hole in the ground, a portal to the rich Jewish past of a city once called the “Jerusalem of the North.”For the first time since 1940, they can see the polished, colorful floor and entire prayer platform of the Great Synagogue of Vilna, built in the 17th century, which became one the most important religious, cultural and intellectual hubs for Diaspora Jews.In Lithuania's small remaining Jewish community, who number less than 3,000, there is no debate that the site must be preserved. But discussions about how to protect the past, and what to build over it, have triggered pain over one of the last pillars of identity left standing for Lithuanian Jews.The community's main representative body plans to build a new Jewish community center over the excavation, where visitors could view the Great Synagogue floor through a glass layer or a basement-level exhibit. Above, the center would celebrate current-day Jewish life through cultural, social and educational events. Some Orthodox Jews and their supporters oppose that project, saying the synagogue should be rebuilt as a house of worship or preserved as a purely archaeological exhibit. Other residents say the mission of a new building should be broadened beyond Lithuanian Jews, offering a center that promotes tolerance, human rights and understanding of Jewish history among all Lithuanians. Lithuanian Jewry was decimated in HolocaustOn the eve of World War II, the massive Great Synagogue stood among more than 100 synagogues and Jewish prayer houses in Vilnius, where about 40% of people were Jewish.Over 90% of Lithuanian Jews were killed in the Holocaust, and from 1944 until 1990, Vilnius was remade as the capital of the Soviet Lithuanian Republic. The synagogue was burned and largely destroyed by the Nazis, then razed by the Soviets to build a school in its place. “This is the place that half the population would have identified their city with,” Jon Seligman, the archaeologist leading the excavation, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “So this city at the moment is missing half its identity, and because it's such a long time since it happened, they don't even know they're missing half their identity.”The excavation is over a decade in the making. Seligman, an Israel-based archaeologist whose Jewish grandparents lived in Lithuania before World War II, first proposed unearthing the synagogue's remains in 2013 after a visit to discover his family roots. His team of archaeologists have worked there since 2015, and last year, the former Soviet school building over the site was demolished. In an accident of history, the synagogue's main floor was constructed below ground and spared from total erasure. “When the building was built in the 17th century, part of the restrictions that were placed on the Jewish community was that they were not allowed to build their synagogue higher than any of the churches in the surroundings,” said Seligman. “So to create the internal majesty, if you don't want to have a low, two-story building, what you do is you drop the floor level one story below ground surface, and that's what they did.”The latest installment of Seligman's project, completed in July, fully exposed this main hall and the bimah, or prayer platform, covered in red, white, green and black geometric designs. Archaeologists also found traces of the Shulhoyf, a busy complex that formed the heartbeat of Jewish life. Vilnius was a major center of Jewish thought, famed for both its religious tradition and modern secular Jewish culture. It was home to the 18th-century Vilna Gaon, one of the most influential Jewish sages, and also the birthplace of the Jewish Labour Bund, a secular, socialist and anti-Zionist organization. Schools taught literature and the sciences in Yiddish and Hebrew, and Zionists shared ideas alongside anti-Zionists. Before World War II, the Shulhoyf hosted 12 prayer houses, a bathhouse, kosher butcher stalls, the first public toilets in Vilnius, the prestigious Strashun Library and the first headquarters of the Yiddish Scientific Institute, or YIVO. That institute, now in New York City, continues to preserve the Yiddish language and cultural heritage of Eastern European Jews. Faina Kukliansky, who has since 2013 chaired the umbrella organization known as the Lithuanian Jewish Community, spearheaded the initiative to construct a community center over the synagogue. Kukliansky grew up as the child of Holocaust survivors in Lithuania under the Soviets. She said the new space will replace the community's current headquarters, hosted in a nearby building that is more than a century old and struggles with heating and water system issues. Kukliansky said the new center will honor both the past and the present of Lithuanian Jews, featuring a YIVO exhibition alongside concerts, social clubs and Jewish learning events. After the Holocaust and decades of Soviet restrictions on Jewish life, those who remain are mostly secular and distant from Jewish traditions. Kukliansky said the center's construction over the remains of the Great Synagogue will inspire Jews to trace the threads of their heritage.“It's very meaningful that in the place where the synagogue rose, Jewish life will be intensive because our Jewish community center is there,” said Kukliansky.But Kukliansky's plans have met sharp opponents from other corners of Lithuania's Jewish world. Among the most vocal is Rabbi Sholom Ber Krinsky, an emissary for the Chabad-Lubavitch Orthodox movement who was born in Boston and has lived in Vilnius since 1994. Some Jews believe a community center wouldn't honor the sanctity of the siteKrinsky said that according to Jewish tradition, the Great Synagogue site should not be covered by a building for secular cultural activities, but remain a “living Jewish religious center that continues the learning and the prayer.” “If a site was used as a synagogue, for centuries, in this case, the holiness retains its holiness, and it's proper to respect that holiness,” said Krinsky. “A Jewish community center might be nice, but it certainly doesn't represent the holiness of that site.”Krinsky has for years demanded more money for Chabad projects, which he says would be used for religious services, Jewish education and social welfare programs. He accuses Kukliansky of monopolizing funds granted to Jews by the Lithuanian government as compensation for property stolen during the Holocaust. The Good Will Foundation, an international body created through the World Jewish Restitution Organization and the Lithuanian Jewish Community, has been authorized to distribute this restitution money. Since legislation passed by the Lithuanian parliament in 2022, the Good Will Foundation has disbursed about $9 million to compensate individual Holocaust survivors and their heirs for private property claims. Given that most Jewish property was left without any heirs, another $40 million is being allocated to support Jewish communal life — including projects like the new community center.Krinsky said these funds have not been sufficiently used to nourish religious life. Kukliansky countered that her organization supports the Choral Synagogue, the only synagogue still active in Lithuania, where Krinsky leads the small group of Jews who usually scrape together a minyan — the minimum of 10 people required for public prayers.Compared with other Eastern European communities, Chabad's footprint is small in Vilnius, where the Vilna Gaon led a tradition of opposing Hasidism that became central to the identity of many Lithuanian Jews. Kukliansky also claims that Krinsky has refused to provide her with financial reports. His wife, Nechama Dina Krinsky, was indicted for tax fraud in 2023.Kukliansky faces further criticism from Dovid Katz, an American-born, Vilnius-based scholar of Yiddish and the Holocaust. Katz advocated for rebuilding the Great Synagogue or preserving its remnants as a religious site, which he said would draw Orthodox pilgrims from around the world. “A synagogue is a religious place, and religious leaders today, and everyday religious Jews, need to be consulted on what's going to replace the Great Synagogue,” said Katz. “It is a place either for a replacement synagogue or for archeological remains.” Still other critics say the Jewish representative body has split the site from a broader mission that would attract non-Jewish Lithuanians and Jews from around the world. Anna Avidan, who founded a nonprofit called Jerusalem of the North to celebrate Jewish history in Lithuania, led a conference in 2017 that invited historians, architects and students to discuss the future of a space commemorating the Great Synagogue. Avidan said attendees proposed a cultural center that would host forums about tolerance, drawing international visitors and educating Lithuanians about the Jewish past of their country. She argued it would be “selfish” to build a center exclusively for the Lithuanian Jewish community, since such spaces are closed to the public, partly for security reasons. The proposals emerging from Avidan's conference were shut down after Kukliansky's opposition.“We are still working on how to include Jewish history in Lithuanian history,” said Avidan. “Approaching the site as a site of Lithuanian history, that would promote this harmony and understanding.” At the excavation site, Seligman's team has dug up pieces of life in the synagogue, which seated about 500 people, with some 500 more squeezing in for High Holidays.The latest artifacts to emerge from the ground include a Passover plate, a dish for gefilte fish, a plaque engraved with the Ten Commandments and several seating plaques with the names of people who donated to the synagogue, assuring their spots inside.These name plaques left clues about families who vanished from Vilnius. One marked a seat for Gitel Klachek, identified as the “wife of the late Yechezkel, Shamash d'Mata,” the city sexton. Their wealthy, influential family owned several businesses around the Great Synagogue.On the uncovered synagogue floor and the surrounding Jewish neighborhoods, there walked people who disputed religion, Jewish identity, Zionism and other ideas. “There would have been a large contingent who would have been ultra-Orthodox. There also would have been a large contingent who were completely secular,” said Seligman. “So the city was very, very much a very mixed community.”The fights over the memory of these ghosts, and over Lithuania's Jewish identity, echo the disagreements that animated the Jews who once thrived there.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cre4.text: Image source, EPA By Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter Published 1 hour ago Nearly six months after US President Donald Trump vowed a swift victory over Iran, the conflict appears to be at a standstill, with prospects of a military victory or negotiated settlement growing dimmer. To break the deadlock, Trump has vowed an "economic D-Day" under which any country that does business with Iran would face "tremendous" economic consequences. Iran, however, has long faced sanctions and has so far shown a willingness to endure pain and a capacity to adapt to immense economic and military pressure as the conflict drags on. The key question for the US then becomes, will further sanctions work where other strategies have failed? The exact mechanics of the new US economic pressure campaign remain unclear, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent promising to reveal them in a news conference on 24 August. But in an interview with CNBC, Bessent made clear that the US is willing to take action against any country - friend or foe - that it believes is extending a lifeline to Iran. "You are either with us or against us," he said. "If you insist on doing business with [Iran], either transferring money, buying their oil or doing seaborne sea transfers, then the US treasury and the US government... will put its full might and force toward enforcing against you." Vice-President JD Vance has described the sanctions as a "new phase" of the conflict in which economic pressure is the "most effective" tool available to the US. "They're going to try to apply economic pressure to us, but what has been true over the last couple of weeks is that they felt a lot more pressure than we have," Vance said on the Clay Travis and Buck Sexton show. "We're going to keep that going because we think that's the best way to ultimately achieve the final objective," he added. Iran has faced significant US sanctions since nearly the beginning of the Islamic Republic in 1979. The economic pressure campaign intensified after the first Trump administration withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), a 2015 pact between world powers and Iran to curb its nuclear programme. And in the current conflict, the US government has already announced Operation Economic Fury, a two-pronged US economic campaign combining US treasury-co-ordinated sanctions against regime financial flows and a naval blockade against Iranian ports. Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, told the BBC the latest announcement was likely the result of mounting frustration that other options have not delivered the results Trump wants. "This is really a recognition that the US is almost stuck in this war," he said. "It's another try at economic pressure." "This is just another tool that the US is using," Bayoumi added. "We've not seen a clear strategy laid out by the administration with either military or economic tools. The question of what the US is trying to achieve is still unanswered." Michael Parker, an eight-year veteran of the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and expert on economic sanctions, said the new strategy will likely represent an effort to "expand the economic blast radius" of sanctions by targeting third countries that still deal with Iran, but have economies that depend on the US dollar. "Thus far, the US has largely used the threat of these secondary sanctions against foreign financial institutions to encourage compliance with sanctions policy," he said. "But this is a lever that is sort of unexplored insofar as targeting anything touching the US dollar that is also touching Iran," Parker added. As an example, Parker pointed to foreign financial institutions that help Iran evade sanctions, or directs money towards Iranian coffers. How Iran would respond to these moves remains unclear, but sanctions experts say that Iran has so far proved adept at using irregular channels to circumvent sanctions - such as "shadow" vessels transporting oil or new commercial fronts unlisted by US sanctions. "You keep seeing new names popping up, because Iran is adapting really quickly," said Mohammed Hammouda, an export control and sanctions manager at the London Stock Exchange. "Whatever sanctions one does, they find a new road [around it]." These Iranian counter-moves, he added, often leave those charged with enforcing compliance playing a game of catch-up. "Sanctions are all on paper, but the hard work is behind the scenes," Hammouda added. "There are teams worldwide trying to impose sanctions and identify those parties involved, which is why Iran has to try to adapt." How effective these sanctions are will largely be determined by how the countries that are ultimately targeted - which could include US allies like Turkey and Iraq, as well as China - react. "Some of this is out of Iran's hands," Parker said. "Iran's ability to evade or avoid sanctions is, in large part, contingent on other countries and financial institution's willingness to give them [Iran] access to the formal banking system." Parker believes that the sanctions are "only as powerful" as the willingness of targeted countries to comply with American foreign policy objectives, or face potentially painful sanctions on trade involving the US dollar. Some experts question whether that willingness currently exists. "I can't really see China agreeing to that, for example," Bayoumi said. "These states have all been able to navigate their own interests with the Trump administration." "The underlying point is that this is just another tool," he added. "But the broader question of strategy remains. Absent that, I'm not sure this is going to change anything long term." https://www.techtimes.com/articles/32652.text: When Netflix dropped the official East of Eden trailer September 2 for its seven-episode adaptation, the shot that landed hardest was almost certainly the quietest: Florence Pugh, as Cathy Ames, delivering the novel's most famous passage in a whisper — not from a narrator's condescending distance, but from the inside. "I believe there are monsters born in this world to human parents." That is Steinbeck's language, reassigned from omniscient judgment to first-person narration — and in that reassignment lies the sharpest creative decision showrunner Zoe Kazan has made. But there is a second layer here, one the trailer does not announce: the series arriving on October 1 will stage, across seven episodes, a debate between three translation choices for a single Hebrew word — and that debate turns out to be where contemporary neuroscience and 3,000-year-old scripture are, quietly, arguing about the same thing.The word is timshel. Or rather: the word is timshol. That distinction, it turns out, is not pedantic. It is the thread that runs from a 1951 correspondence between a novelist and a talmudic genius, through Benjamin Libet's 1983 EEG laboratory, to Robert Sapolsky's 2023 demolition of free will — and it is still standing on the other side.What Kazan's East of Eden Is Actually AboutThe Trask family's story spans the American Civil War through World War I, set in California's Salinas Valley — a geography Steinbeck chose with intention, among the most fertile agricultural land in the country as the setting for every form of human corruption. The adaptation, filmed in Auckland, Dunedin, Oamaru in New Zealand, stars Christopher Abbott as Adam Trask, Mike Faist as his brother Charles, and Florence Pugh — also an executive producer — as Cathy Ames, whose violent arrival in the Trask household sets the multigenerational catastrophe in motion.Joseph Zada plays Cal Trask and Joe Anders plays his twin Aron — the sons whose lives will reenact, in miniature, the story of Cain and Abel that structures the entire novel. Hoon Lee, Ciarán Hinds, Tracy Letts, and Martha Plimpton round out a cast Kazan has assembled for a fundamentally different creative project from the celebrated 1955 James Dean adaptation directed by her grandfather Elia Kazan: not a historical drama that happens to use the Cain-Abel myth, but a direct examination of what that myth is actually claiming about human nature.Zoe Kazan has described the series as needing to be "epic and intimate," and the trailer's opening — Pugh narrating her own condition with the focused, affectless clarity of a forensic examiner — signals which of those two registers will drive the series' engine. This is not the warm nostalgia of historical fiction. It is an investigation.Cathy's story, as Steinbeck wrote it and as Kazan has chosen to center it, begins before the Trask family does: a young woman who experiences the world as a predation problem to be solved, whose violence is neither remorseful nor impulsive but strategic, and who arrives at the Trask farm after an act of destruction so severe the novel treats it as barely explicable. She marries Adam, abandons her sons, and becomes the story's adversarial input — the proof-of-concept that what the novel will call timshel is meaningful, because Cathy appears constitutionally unable to use it.Timshel, Timshol, and the Lithuanian Rabbi Who Changed American LiteratureThe most important word in Steinbeck's novel does not exist in Hebrew.In Genesis 4:7, God warns Cain before Abel's murder with a clause whose translation determines everything: whether Cain is promised victory over sin, commanded to achieve it, or merely offered the possibility. The King James Version renders this as "thou shalt rule over him," a promise; the American Standard Bible as "do thou rule over him," a command; and in Steinbeck's retelling, through the character Lee after years of study with Hebrew scholars, as "thou mayest" — a grant of possibility. That translation is attributed to the Hebrew word "timshel."The problem, as scholar Sheila Tuller Keiter documented in careful philological detail for the Jewish Review of Books (Fall 2022), is that "timshel" is not, technically, a Hebrew word. The word in the Masoretic text is timshol (תִּמְשָׁל) — the second-person masculine singular future form of the verb mashal, meaning to rule or govern. The tav prefix signals "you, singular masculine, future tense." The remaining letters — mem, shin, lamed — form the Hebrew root for ruling, control, governance. Timshol means, most literally, "you will rule."How did Steinbeck arrive at his spelling and his translation? The answer runs through one of the most consequential games of exegetical telephone in American literary history. Steinbeck's editor at Viking Press, Pascal Covici — himself a Romanian-born Jew — consulted on the novelist's behalf with Professor Louis Ginzberg of the Jewish Theological Seminary, the preeminent Talmudic scholar of his generation, whose best-known work The Legends of the Jews remains an invaluable resource. Ginzberg was born in Kovno, Lithuania, in 1873 and brought with him a Litvish, or Lithuanian, Hebrew accent — a regional variant in which the "oh" sound characteristic of the Ashkenazic tradition morphs into an "ey" sound. Timshol, spoken in Ginzberg's Litvish accent, would have sounded something like "timsheyl." Steinbeck, receiving the word through Covici's relay, wrote it as "timshel."The mistransliteration is documented. Steinbeck wrote Covici that he was not entirely satisfied with Ginzberg's reading — that he might need to "go outside of rabbinical thought to pure scholarship which may be non-Jewish," distinguishing theology from etymology. He never fully resolved the question. The word carved into the wooden manuscript box he gave Covici when he finished writing does not exist in Hebrew.And yet — Keiter's own conclusion, and the novel's enduring resonance, suggest that the mistransliteration produced something more philosophically acute than the accurate text would have. The future tense of mashal does carry, at the grammatical level, the flavor of possibility rather than certainty. It does not guarantee conquest of sin. It does not command it. It describes what might happen, given the architecture of human agency. Lee's reading — "thou mayest" — is not a philological precision, but it is a philosophical one.Sapolsky Attacks Free Will. Timshel Was Never Defending That.In 2023, Stanford neuroscientist and primatologist Robert Sapolsky published a 528-page hard determinism argument — Determined: A Science of Life Without Free Will — contending that human behavior is entirely the product of biology, prior experience, and environment, leaving no genuine space for the kind of free will that would ground moral responsibility. Sapolsky's position is what philosophers call hard incompatibilism: the view that free will and determinism are mutually exclusive, and that determinism wins.His central neuroscientific anchor is Libet's 1983 readiness potential experiments — in which measured brain activity preceding voluntary movement appeared approximately 200 to 550 milliseconds before participants reported conscious awareness of their intention to move. The brain, in this reading, has already initiated the action before the conscious mind registers the decision.The Libet finding has been contested. Neuroscientist Aaron Schurger proposed that what Libet measured may in fact be neural background noise at threshold — not a decision, but a random fluctuation being interpreted after the fact. Regardless of how the Libet debate resolves, however, there is a more fundamental problem with treating Sapolsky's argument as a challenge to Timshel.Sapolsky is attacking libertarian free will: the philosophical position that at the moment of choice, the agent is the uncaused cause of her action — that there is some space in the causal chain where the self steps in and overrides biology, environment, and neural architecture. That is the position neuroscience does undermine. But it is not the position Steinbeck's "thou mayest" was ever defending.What Timshel actually asserts is something closer to what philosophers call compatibilism, the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism. The philosophical tradition running from Hobbes ("freedom consists in finding no stop in doing what one has the will to do") through David Hume, Harry Frankfurt's hierarchical theory of desire, and P.F. Strawson's analysis of reactive attitudes has argued, for centuries, that the freedom relevant to moral responsibility does not require being an uncaused cause. It requires acting from one's own values and reasoning in a way that is responsive to reasons — without external compulsion. A person who chooses, even in a causally determined universe, by running her genuine values through her deliberative capacities, and who could act differently if she had different reasons, is free in every sense that matters for moral accountability.When Adam Trask, dying, whispers "timshel" to Cal, he is not asserting that Cal is metaphysically uncaused. He is asserting that the door is still open — that within the causal structure Cal inhabits, including the biological pressure from his mother's nature and whatever epigenetic marks that inheritance has left, the capacity for deliberate action guided by his own values is real and sufficient for moral agency. That is a compatibilist claim. And compatibilism, as the Stanford Encyclopedia confirms, is not the view neuroscience has undermined.Sapolsky is arguing against a position that academic philosophy already largely abandoned. Steinbeck's Timshel was never defending that position. The conflict between them, treated as a genuine philosophical confrontation, dissolves when you know what compatibilism is.Cathy Ames and the Limits of TimshelThe series' most intellectually honest move — and Kazan's most genuinely difficult creative commitment — is that it takes seriously the possibility that Timshel does not apply equally to everyone.Contemporary clinical psychology would describe Cathy's presentation as primary psychopathy: low emotional reactivity, an absence of guilt or empathy, high predatory intelligence, and an instrumental relationship to other people. These are not character descriptions but neurological ones. Neuroimaging studies have documented that psychopathy is associated with measurably reduced uncinate fasciculus structural integrity — the primary white matter pathway connecting the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), the region responsible for empathy and guilt, with the amygdala, which mediates fear and emotional responsiveness. Both diffusion tensor imaging and functional MRI have confirmed diminished vmPFC connectivity and less coordinated activity between these regions in individuals with psychopathic traits.These are not choices. They are architecture.If Cathy's moral blindness has a neurological substrate — if the vmPFC-amygdala circuit that normally integrates emotional context into moral judgment is structurally compromised — then Timshel's invitation presents differently to her than it does to Cal. The question the novel asks, and the series inherits: can someone choose good if the brain is not architecturally equipped to value it?Frankfurt's hierarchical compatibilism offers one angle on this question: acting of one's own free will means acting from desires one endorses at a higher order of reflection — from one's will as one wishes it to be. Cathy does act from desires she endorses. She is not acting against herself. But philosopher Susan Wolf's Reason View pushes further: for blameworthy conduct, an agent must be able to act in accordance with the True and the Good — not merely with whatever her psychology currently values. A structural deficit in the neural substrate for empathy raises the possibility that the relevant responsiveness to reasons is itself architecturally limited.Steinbeck's own answer, embedded in the novel's structure, is that Timshel is primarily for everyone else: for Adam, who chooses to believe in Cathy; for Cal, who chooses not to become her; for Aron, whose choice fails. Cathy functions as the system's adversarial input — the proof-of-concept that freedom to choose goodness is real, precisely because her incapacity to exercise it is visible.Kazan's recentering of the narrative in Cathy's perspective refuses the comfort of that distance. From inside Cathy's consciousness, the question becomes: what does the world look like from a mind that is genuinely differently structured? Not to excuse what Cathy does — the series, from the trailer, is not heading toward rehabilitation — but to refuse the easy condemnation of a being who may not have been given the same moral toolkit the rest of us take for granted. That is a more contemporary question than Steinbeck's omniscient narrator could ask. It is a question the neuroscience of psychopathy, thirty years of vmPFC-amygdala research, has made it possible to ask with real clinical specificity.What the Salinas Valley Is Doing in New ZealandSteinbeck's Salinas Valley is not merely a setting — it is a philosophical argument structured as landscape. A place of extraordinary agricultural abundance that hosts every form of human corruption. Eden — generous, beautiful, governed by sun and water — and its inhabitants already east of it, already after the fall, already carrying the inheritance of Cain.The production choice to film in New Zealand's South Island is worth a moment's attention. Dunedin and Oamaru offer 19th-century Europeanized built environment and pastoral terrain that can plausibly stand in for turn-of-the-century California, but the substitution also lends the production a quality of estrangement — an America seen from outside itself — that aligns with Kazan's ambition.The novel's temporal frame — American Civil War to World War I — was not incidental to Steinbeck. The Civil War is the moment America confronted the consequences of inherited sin at a civilizational scale. World War I is the violent erasure of Edenic innocence that ended the era in which any version of the old moral certainties could survive. The Trask and Hamilton generations are living out, in domestic microcosm, exactly the half-century in which America lost the ability to pretend its inherited wounds were not wounds.What Kazan adds, in making this a 2026 series rather than a 1952 novel or a 1955 film, is the contemporary biological question: what do we now know about what gets handed down? The epigenetics of intergenerational trauma, the neuroscience of psychopathy, the contested science of moral agency — these are not the conceptual vocabulary Steinbeck had access to. They are the vocabulary his central question was always reaching for. "What gets handed down? What are you carrying? How do we reconcile ourselves with our shadow selves?" Kazan has said. The biological sciences now have partial answers to all three questions. Timshel, properly understood, is still compatible with every one of them.Does Timshel Apply to Cal Trask?The novel's answer is: yes, conditionally, specifically, and at enormous cost.Cal knows his history. He fears it. He enacts it. And at the novel's end — when his dying father whispers "timshel" — the word does not erase the biological pressures or the neurological architecture of whatever Cal has inherited. It insists, with parental authority, that the door has not yet closed. Not because Cal is uncaused. Not because his choices float free of biology. But because compatibilist agency — acting from one's values within a causally structured world, remaining genuinely responsive to reasons, capable of being held accountable — is real, and real in a way that does not require any particular neurological architecture to remain uncaused.That is what Steinbeck was reaching for in the mistransliterated Hebrew word that a Lithuanian rabbi's accent

(Photo by YASUYOSHI CHIBA / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Polish authorities suggest Russian intelligence is to blame for a recent fire at a Starlink ground station in central Poland. The fire damaged the power plant and generator in Wola Krobowska, located in the Masovian Voivodeship about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Warsaw, causing the station to lose its internet connection and disrupting access for several organizations, including the Ukrainian military. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Przemysław Nowak, a spokesman for the Polish National Prosecutor’s Office, said the police have “reasonable suspicion” that Russian intelligence is behind the fire, according to Polish outlet TVP World on Friday. “There is... reasonable suspicion that the perpetrators acted on the orders of Russian special services and on behalf of a foreign intelligence service against the Republic of Poland,” Nowak said. Advertisement “The aim of their actions was to disrupt Starlink internet traffic and communications in Poland and other countries of Central and Eastern Europe,” he added. While Starlink satellites relay data to one another, traffic must ultimately be routed through ground stations to connect to terrestrial networks and data centers. Krzysztof Gawkowski, Poland’s deputy prime minister and digital affairs minister, also voiced similar suspicions in his remarks on Thursday. The incident came amid warnings from top Polish officials of intensifying Russian hybrid attacks, including sabotage, against Poland and NATO as a whole, with Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski cautioning that Moscow is planning “ something big ” in 2026 in a recent remark. Other Topics of Interest Fire at Polish Starlink Hub Sparks Sabotage Investigation The incident temporarily disrupted connectivity used across the region, including services supporting Ukraine, and has raised fresh concerns about potential attacks on critical communications infrastructure. Russia has not claimed responsibility for the incident, and the investigation remains open with no arrests made after the station resumed operations. Ukraine’s edge over Russia Ukraine has gained a slight edge in frontline communications over Russia after Kyiv worked with SpaceX to introduce a verification system in February. The verification system has disabled terminals used by Russian troops, and Moscow has since looked for alternatives while disrupting Ukrainian access to Starlink. Advertisement One way for Moscow to remedy the situation is by hiring Ukrainians to illegally register terminals for Russian troops. Earlier this week, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said it detained two men in Lviv for attempting to register more than 50 Starlink accounts on behalf of Russian intelligence agencies. In July, the SBU said it arrested two other men in Kyiv who registered 76 terminals for Russia , then announced a day later that it had arrested another man in central Ukraine’s Dnipro for activating over 1,000 Starlink terminals for Russia. Another is to target nodes that support the system. On Saturday morning, Russia’s defense ministry claimed to have hit a data center in Kyiv that “provided mobile internet service and support for the Starlink satellite communications system for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.” Russia has also tried to remedy the issue by introducing alternatives , including its domestically deployed Rassvet satellites. The Rassvet has had some success – namely, a twice-daily communication window over Ukraine by August – but is marred by deployment hurdles, with the limited number of satellites in orbit made worse by failed launches that sent their already limited numbers plummeting back to Earth . https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/10/17/kata.text: Menü Kereső Feljelentést tett Kátai-Németh Vilmos, közpénzből is mehetett a kampány a fideszes Koncz Zsófia választókerületében Belföld Joób Sándor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Hivatali visszaélés és hűtlen kezelés gyanúja miatt feljelentést tett Kátai-Németh Vilmos szociális és családügyi miniszter a Családbarát Magyarország program 2026 tavaszán Szerencsen finanszírozott rendezvényei miatt – jelentette be a miniszter a Facebook-oldalán közzétett videóban . Idén április 5-én 343 millió forintba került egy húsvéti rendezvény a fideszes Koncz Zsófia volt családügyi államtitkár szerencsi választókerületében, mondta a politikus. Az MTI akkori tudósítása szerint Koncz államtitkárként mondott beszédet egy Szerencsen rendezett húsvéti rendezvényen. Itt „egy kifejezetten családokra épülő programot szerveztek, amelynek része volt a tojáskeresés és számos, a gyermekek számára élményt nyújtó foglalkozás”. Koncz a közmédiának adott interjújában akkor arról beszélt, hogy a költségvetésben „soha nem látott mértékű” támogatás van a családok számára, és felsorolta a kormány családtámogatási intézkedéseit. Kátai-Németh Vilmos a videójában arról beszél, hogy 2026 februárja és az országgyűlési választások között, alig két hónap alatt több mint 600 millió forint közpénzt fordított a Fidesz-kormány a szerencsi rendezvényekre a Családbarát Magyarország programsorozat keretében. A Szociális és Családügyi Minisztérium szombaton még azt közölte, hogy a választások előtt Szerencsen hat, minisztériumi forrásból finanszírozott eseményt tartottak, amelyeken Koncz Zsófia valamennyi alkalommal megjelent és felszólalt. Az országos programsorozatnak szánt rendezvénysorozat vidéki helyszínei között Szerencs kiemelten támogatottnak minősült. A minisztérium álláspontja szerint ezért tisztázni kell, hogy a rendezvények valóban a családpolitikai célokat szolgálták-e, vagy az állami költségvetésből részben egy országgyűlési képviselőjelölt választási kampányát finanszírozták. Az eseményeket a szerződés alapján egyébként 2026. december 15-ig kitolhatták volna – ám ezt nem tették. A 2026 áprilisi választásokon a Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén megyei 6-os számú, Tiszaújvárosi központú választókerületében a tiszás Bihari Zoltán a szavazatok 51,2 százalékával nyerte meg a választást. A fideszes Koncz Zsófia 43,2 százalékot kapott, de listáról bekerült az országgyűlésbe. Ahogy a Telexen megírtuk , Koncz Zsófia, a KIM családokért felelős államtitkára tavaly novemberben jelentette be, hogy a „Családbarát Magyarország” program keretében minden vidéki bölcsődébe visznek műanyag kismotorokat a gyerekeknek. A „családbarát” matricával ellátott játékokat a Hankó Balázs által vezetett Kulturális és Innovációs Minisztérium közpénzből vásárolt meg. A minisztérium akkor azt közölte, hogy „közel 55 ezer gyermekhez jutnak el az eszközök”. Az Átlátszó megkereste a minisztérium családbarát programjára vonatkozó szerződést, ami nettó 2,8 milliárd forintos keretről szólt , a megállapodást 2025. november 18-án írta alá a KIM a Balásy Gyula-féle New Land Media Kft.-vel és a Lounge Design Kft.-vel. Később kiderült, hogy a minisztérium összesen 12 ezer kismotort vett Balásy Gyula cégeitől nettó 185,3 millió forintért, és még 3 millió forint volt a járgányok felmatricázása. Ez azt jelenti, hogy egy darabért több mint 15 ezer forint közpénzt fizettek a Balásy-cégeknek, ami háromszoros túlárazás, hiszen egy ilyen kismotor a legtöbb helyen nagyjából 5-6 ezer forintért kapható .
